#7529. OpenAI’s New Shopping Strategy; What Advertisers Are Thankful For

Sometimes, momentous change happens in the most banal ways.

So it was last week when OpenAI made an unheralded change to its “Shopping with ChatGPT Search” documentation, as AI Visibility Journal reports.

The documentation previously read: “Product results are selected independently by ChatGPT and are not ads, nor influenced by any OpenAI partnerships.” Now it reads: “Product results are not ads; how products and merchants are selected is described below.”

The cynical take is that OpenAI is now allowing room for marketing partnerships to influence ChatGPT’s product recommendations, even outside of official ads.

Other changes to the documentation are less important, though telling. ChatGPT formerly committed to showing products with “links to sites where you can learn more or purchase.” Now ChatGPT’s mandate is only to “show available ways to purchase.”

Marketers and merchants want to influence how their products and brands are presented to AI search users. There’s massive demand for such services (which are called AEO or GEO, as an evolution of SEO).

Plus, some platforms that are essential for AI training are monetizing their influence over the chatbots. Amazon recently launched “Conversational Briefs” – a silly underwear-adjacent name for a product that lets brands pay to affect relevant AI search outputs.

But AI platforms themselves are hesitant to break the dam and let brands pay to boost their profile directly. Which could look like, for instance, businesses picking and choosing which customer reviews get surfaced or considered by the model, or pay-to-play prompts or keywords.

Holiday ads might be creeping into the schedule earlier than ever this year, but don’t get it twisted: For a lot of TV advertisers, broadcasters and streamers, Thanksgiving weekend is the main event.

On Thursday, NBCUniversal has the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, the National Dog Show and one of three Thanksgiving NFL games (CBS and Fox will broadcast the other two). Meanwhile, on Wednesday, Netflix has the first-ever Thanksgiving Eve NFL game, and Prime Video is airing its first Duke men’s college basketball game. Then, on Black Friday, Prime has a 15-hour marathon of live sports coverage lined up, including an NFL game, two Emirates NBA Cup games and a PGA golf event.

All that TV makes this weekend a crucial one for advertisers. Not only are many more people watching live during the Thanksgiving weekend (a record 34 million watched the Macy’s parade last year), but the National Retail Federation estimates that 182.7 million are planning to shop then, too.

Which means it’s one of the rare times when TV is both a massive brand awareness play and short-term performance driver.

It’s no wonder, then, that both NBC and Amazon are leaning heavily into interactive ad formats for their streaming broadcasts this year, as Variety reports. Amazon’s ads will feature on-screen prompts for interacting with Alexa or adding items straight to a customer’s Amazon cart, while Peacock will present shoppable pause ads that set up Instacart deliveries for users.

Ruh-roh: Loads of ad dollars are still getting lost in the programmatic abyss.

Only 43.1% of programmatic spend made it to “quality media” last quarter, according to the latest ANA Programmatic Transparency Benchmark report. The research says that, for every $1 million of programmatic ad spend, more than half is lost to transaction costs ($285,000) and media productivity ($284,000).

Ad tech taxes aren’t solely to blame for the wasted spend, though. The lack of effective measurement is also a significant source of programmatic inefficiency, according to the ANA. And poor measurement standards are a “particularly acute” problem in connected TV environments, where a whopping 24% of ad spend went to “non-measurable inventory.”

While the report doesn’t clearly define what makes inventory non-measurable, it’s no secret that CTV ad measurement is murky, to say the very least. Publishers, agencies and measurement and currency vendors can hardly agree on how to count reach, let alone how to quantify outcomes.

Sounds like those buy-side demands for more transparency are about to get even louder.

Would you watch a 24/7 personalized AI TV channel about yourself? Because Google’s trying to patent that technology right now. [404 Media]

Don’t write off DSPs in the age of agentic advertising. [Adweek]

Microsoft search advertisers can now extend their campaigns into the Pinterest search platform. [Ad Age]

After Jensen Huang’s unceremonious departure from NVIDIA amid affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and multiple subordinates, the company has appointed its new CEO: Jensen Huang. [TechCrunch]

Agentic advertising platform BrandComms.ai promotes Sheona Richard from chief client officer to CEO. [post]

CX platform Emplifi appoints Claire Wilson as chief marketing officer. [blog]

Stravito uses a variety of data sources to build out AI personas for different audiences, and touts a “glass box” approach to AI.

Philips Sonicare, a maker of electric toothbrushes and water flossers, decided to consolidate its streaming TV ad buys within Amazon, which has also been doing some consolidating itself.

After selling ads at The Wall Street Journal and WebMD and rising to CRO at The Trade Desk, Jed Dederick is now the first-ever chief revenue officer of creator startup ShopMy.

DecryptAds’ goal, Garcia said, is to give researchers, ad agencies, tech companies and regulators the evidence they need to fix security gaps in the programmatic supply chain.

The mobile growth marketing platform Liftoff reported its second-ever quarterly earnings last week. Shares were up by almost 25% after the company exceeded its revenue target and projected an optimistic profit margin outlook moving forward.

CTV sellers are promising measurable outcomes – even guaranteed store visits – but winning advertiser trust takes more than just measurement.

#7528. Weird animals win on Instagram. Mongabay’s next-best choice? Its reporters.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories.’”

Mongabay’s most successful videos are about weird animals.

But not every video from the environmental newsroom can be about strange — or strangely cute — animals. Some have to be about shrimp farm pollution. Or a deforestation crisis brought on by cacao farming in Liberia. That’s where the challenge comes in, Mongabay video managing editor Lucia Torres has found. Turning that kind of journalism into something people stop scrolling for isn’t easy.

“Generally mass audiences are less interested in environmental content on YouTube [and] Instagram,” Torres said. “We have to compete with recipes, music videos, etc.”

Mongabay publishes around 150 to 200 videos a year with a team of four full-time and one half-time producers. These include short vertical videos on YouTube Shorts and Instagram; evergreen explainers around “complex enviro-problems”; twice-monthly features; and lengthy investigations or short documentaries.

To reach new audiences with its environmental journalism, Mongabay started experimenting with behind-the-scenes reels in late 2024. At the time, Mongabay’s Instagram reels averaged 2,000 to 3,000 views. Torres said she was inspired by behind-the-scenes videos from National Geographic, The New York Times, ProPublica, and contributing creator Izzy Sasada. An early behind-the-scenes video — on pollution from those shrimp farms — drew about 14,000 views. Additional videos from California and Indonesia each got about 6,000 views. Mongabay started to dive deeper with videos that featured sources and reporters filming from the field.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

From the initial tests, it became clear to Torres that the best-performing videos were ones with behind-the-scenes footage from investigations or collaborations. Putting reporters on camera — in the field or at their desks — worked.

“The content [on platforms like Instagram] is dominated now by individual content creators,” said Torres, who is currently a Knight Science Journalism Fellow at MIT. She said Mongabay is “still figuring out how we can create personalities or creators within the organization that represent what Mongabay does — that are good journalists but also good at talking in front of the camera.”

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Another successful example came with Mongabay’s investigation into vanishing forests in Liberia. The piece ran as a long-form article, a lengthy YouTube video, and a behind-the-scenes short.

A post shared by Mongabay | mongabay.com (@mongabay)

Mongabay now plans its multimedia packages for big investigative stories from the beginning. “They require cross-team, high-level collaborations,” Torres said. “You really have to think about all the elements you are going to use before starting production so when you’re in the field you get everything you need.”

Not everything has panned out. Last year, Mongabay tried a data visualization series on climate data. It didn’t work. The lessons for the newsroom went beyond video.

“People are sick and tired of doomer content, and they also don’t like ‘climate stories,’” Torres said. “The simple mention of ‘climate’ scares them away.”

CEO and founder Rhett Butler has seen the same thing across Mongabay’s journalism.

“We’re seeing strong evidence that doomer stories are resonating less with our audiences,” he said. “Climate stories — especially those focused on disasters or the climate emergency — tend to garner less interest than other topics.” The ones that do well, he added, have “an ecosystem or wildlife angle, give readers a sense of agency, or present a solution.”

Mongabay has responded by introducing more projects and series focused on solutions journalism, like Indigenous-led conservation, agroecology, and conservation technology.

RELATED ARTICLEAudience editors offer advice for “dispiriting” times in social and searchSarah ScireJanuary 16, 2025“We’ve also been sharing data with the newsroom about which kinds of framing are reaching more people right now, so writers and editors can consider whether they might want to incorporate how people are responding to problems into their stories,” Butler said. “But we aren’t overly prescriptive, so ultimately it’s up to editors and writers how they use this information.”

Looking at the 3,422 articles published between June 1, 2025 and August 31, 2026, Butler found that the median story featuring hope or a solution got 41% more traffic than articles that only described the crisis or threat. (Articles classified as being about an “action confronting a threat” got 43% more.)

Today, 71% of the 100 most-read stories on Mongabay’s English-language site can be classified as “hope / solution / agency” or “action confronting a threat,” Butler said. Only 21% were “doom only.”

The video team has done something similar. The environmental newsroom’s short series Stranger Creatures leads with “the wonder of wild creatures first,” Torres noted. The conservation or endangered species angle follows.

“We’ve stopped framing stories as a climate problem, and started framing stories from a solutions-oriented, action-driven perspective, community-first, or fun-stuff first,” Torres said. “Climate is implicit now in the stories.”

What video won’t be, at least for now, is a revenue generator. Almost all of Mongabay’s revenue comes from contributions and grants, according to its annual report. (Events, licensing, and advertising “are insignificant at this point,” Butler said.)

“I’m not bullish on video becoming a material source of revenue for Mongabay, given how the space has evolved and our position in it,” Butler said. “Ten years ago I was a lot more optimistic on that front.”

Part of the problem, he said, is incentives. “Building a video strategy around advertising creates an incentive to prioritize views, which may not align with our broader organizational emphasis on impact,” Butler said. “The stories that attract the largest audiences aren’t necessarily those most likely to inform decisions or prompt action.”

#7526. Court to hear argument on whether school employees may bring suit under Title IX

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

The federal law known as Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination by schools that receive federal funding. On November 30, the Supreme Court will hear oral argument in a dispute over whether the law allows school employees to bring lawsuits alleging sex discrimination, or whether such employees must instead rely on a different federal law, Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, that specifically provides a remedy for sex-based employment discrimination but also imposes constraints not found in Title IX. The employees seeking to bring the lawsuits under Title IX will face a bench that has become increasingly reluctant to permit private plaintiffs to bring lawsuits unless the federal statute at issue clearly authorizes them.

The plaintiffs in the case are two former employees of Georgia’s state university system. Thomas Crowther worked as an art professor at Augusta University. When he was accused of inappropriate conduct by several students, including sexual harassment, the university initially suspended him for one semester and then declined to renew his contract, prompting Crowther to file a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

Machelle Joseph was the head women’s basketball coach at Georgia Tech. She was fired in 2019 after an investigation raised concerns about mistreatment of players. Before her termination, Joseph had repeatedly complained about her team receiving fewer resources than the men’s team. Joseph filed a lawsuit against the university for sex discrimination and retaliation.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit considered Crowther’s and Joseph’s cases together. It held that Title IX does not provide a right – either explicitly or by implication – for employees to sue for sex discrimination. When the full court declined to reconsider their case, Crowther and Joseph asked the Supreme Court to weigh in, which it agreed in May to do.

Crowther and Joseph urge the justices to reverse the 11th Circuit’s decision and allow their lawsuits to go forward. They point to the text of Title IX, which provides that “[n]o person … shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.” That language, they say, creates a broad ban on sex discrimination by schools that receive federal funding; moreover, they add, Title IX “also contains ‘a list of narrow exceptions’ that does not include employment discrimination” – further evidence that Congress intended Title IX’s ban on sex discrimination to apply to both employees and students.

The Georgia university system agrees that Title IX bars sex discrimination in employment, “and that federal agencies may deny funding to violators.” But that is not the question before the court, it stresses. Instead, it emphasizes, the issue is whether Title IX allows employees to bring private lawsuits alleging that they were the victims of sex-based discrimination. The answer, the university system says, is no.

To support their position, Crowther and Joseph cite several past Supreme Court rulings, including its 1982 decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell. In Bell, the court upheld regulations, meant to implement Title IX, that barred sex-based discrimination against employees (as well as students) at federally funded educational institutions. That decision, they say, demonstrates that Title IX prohibits sex-based discrimination in employment. “The Court’s cases, read together,” they continue, “lead to the inexorable conclusion that an employee who is a victim of intentional sex-based discrimination by a federally funded education program or activity has a private right of action to seek damages under Title IX.”

Crowther and Joseph add that the Supreme Court has allowed employment discrimination lawsuits under other federal antidiscrimination statutes that apply to the recipients of federal funds – Title VI of Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color, or national origin, and the Rehabilitation Act of 1973, which prohibits discrimination based on disability. Those laws, they write, contain “virtually identical” language – further evidence that Title IX allows lawsuits like theirs.

The university pushes back against the employees’ attempt to draw comparisons with other federal antidiscrimination laws. It writes that Supreme Court “has assumed,” but has never specifically held, that “Title VI permits private suits for the narrow category of employment discrimination that statute prohibits.” But in any event, it says, that assumption does not indicate anything about whether Congress created a private remedy in Title IX. The university system also emphasizes that “[t]he Rehabilitation Act has always been a far more detailed and targeted statute than Title IX” – for example, it “expressly ban[s] disability discrimination by the federal government as [an] employer.”

Similarly, the university system continues, the Supreme Court’s decision in North Haven Board of Education v. Bell does not resolve the question before the justices now. The court in that case, it writes, “had no reason to, and did not, consider whether Congress created a private remedy atop the express one the challenged regulations implemented.”

Whether the availability of another remedy forecloses private lawsuits under Title IX

The Supreme Court, the university system writes, has made clear that the right to bring a private lawsuit hinges on whether there is “evidence confirming that Congress sought to” provide such a right. And when Congress has created “an express remedy” in another statute, there is “a strong ‘presumption’ that Congress did not imply others” – particularly when that “express remedy” involves a “‘comprehensive’ remedial scheme.”

That is exactly what happened here, the university system argues. “Mere weeks before Congress passed Title IX,” the university contends, “it extended … [the] protection—and reticulated enforcement scheme” in Title VII to school employees, which bars employment discrimination based on (among other things) sex. Therefore, the university system says, allowing lawsuits like Crowther’s and Joseph’s to go forward under Title IX “would attribute to the same Congress an inexplicable about-face: Immediately after giving a set of employees a private employment-discrimination remedy mediated by a ‘detailed administrative and judicial process,’ it silently gave the same employees a second private right of action, to attack the same basic harm.” And it did so, the university system suggests, without requiring employees to comply with any of the “strings attached” to private lawsuits under Title VII – including, but not limited to, the requirement to first file a complaint with the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission before going to court and its limits on the damages that can be recovered.

Crowther and Joseph counter that “Title IX and Title VII are ‘vastly different.’” The prospect “that an employee might be able to bring a claim under both Title IX and Title VII does not justify” a determination that a private right of action is not available under Title IX. Rather, they write, the Supreme Court “has recognized that Congress has enacted overlapping remedies to eradicate employment discrimination, and Congress chose not to exclude employment discrimination from Title IX’s broad reach.”

As additional support for the idea that Title IX does not provide a private right of action for employees, the university system notes that the law was enacted pursuant to Congress’ power under the Constitution’s Spending Clause, which gives Congress the power to impose taxes and spend money for (among other things) the country’s “general welfare.” In exchange for the federal funds, the recipients therefore agree to comply with the conditions that Congress imposes, and Congress can terminate the funding if a recipient fails to do so. However, in cases such as last term’s Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety, the Supreme Court has held that additional sanctions for violating the conditions in a law, such as the ability to bring a private lawsuit, are only available if the recipient has knowingly and voluntarily agreed to those sanctions. Here, the university system asserts, “Title IX does not unambiguously authorize private employment-discrimination suits,” and so it could not have known that it could be sued by employees, much less have agreed to that possibility.

Crowther and Joseph reject this argument. They say that recipients of Title IX funds “‘have been on notice that they could be subjected to private suits for intentional sex discrimination under Title IX since 1979.’” As a result, they write, the Supreme Court’s “Spending Clause precedents ‘do[] not preclude private suits for intentional acts that clearly violate Title IX.’”

A “friend of the court” brief from West Virginia and 20 other states attempts to refute this assertion. The states tell the justices that the states “are best positioned to say what Title IX’s bargain contains, as they’re the ones who’ve accepted it.” And they “can say with firsthand authority that the deal they made did not include this,” they write. “To the contrary, all the circumstances suggested to the States that Title VII [procedures, not private lawsuits] was the rightful home for those cases.”

The Trump administration, which filed a “friend of the court” brief supporting the university system, urges the justices not to reach the Spending Clause question at all. Instead, U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer tells the justices, they “should decide this case on the ground that” the employees’ “claims fail as a matter of ‘statutory interpretation’ alone.” Therefore, he writes, it is “unnecessary to reach, and prudent to avoid, the parties’ further dispute over the constitutional notice requirement for legislation enacted under Congress’s spending power.”

The possible effects of the court’s decision

Both the Trump administration and lawyers representing public school districts warn that a ruling in the employees’ favor could have “significant adverse consequences.” The federal government suggests that allowing lawsuits like the employees’ to go forward “would crowd judicial dockets with premature lawsuits that could often be avoided through proper use of Title VII’s administrative process, which successfully resolves numerous cases. And it would undermine the government’s primary authority to enforce both Title VII … and Title IX.”

For its part, the National School Attorneys Association emphasizes that “public school districts typically operate with limited legal and administrative staff. Expanding Title IX’s implied private right of action to cover claims against employees,” it says, “would impose disproportionate compliance and litigation burdens on public school districts and diminish the limited resources they have to educate students.”

But a brief from the National Education Association, supporting the employees, takes a contrary stance. It tells the justices that upholding the 11th Circuit’s decision “would remove a critical deterrent against sex-based mistreatment of educators, exacerbate an already dire workforce crisis, and ultimately compromise the quality of education available to millions of students nationwide.” Lawsuits under Title VII, it writes, are not enough because that law “does not offer the full protections to which employees of education programs are entitled.”

A decision in the case is expected by late June or early July.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7524. The Onion’s new plan to market its print newspaper: sponsoring a bowl game

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.)

On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:

The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

But we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM

For those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one company or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

Indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.)

Collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently said no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.)

So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The New Orleans Bowl.

I love New Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM

Then the folks who run the New Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM

Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in New Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and said it straight up: "No."

We asked why. They said politics. And the Sickos Guy.

— Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM

While the New Orleans Bowl might be out, several currently-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

#7523. Principal Media Or Unprincipled Media?

According to the ANA, nine in 10 marketers worry that principal media isn’t serving their best interests – and yet more than half of them bought it last year.

It’s a head-scratcher, says Kamran Asghar, global CEO and co-founder of independent media agency Crossmedia, on this Thanksgiving episode of AdExchanger Talks.

“Why we accept this is mind-boggling to me,” he says.

In a principal media deal, an agency isn’t just advising a client; it’s selling to them. The agency buys media in bulk with its own money, then resells it to the client – usually without saying what’s in the package or what it paid – and then keeps the difference.

Which raises an obvious question: Is the agency recommending what’s best for its client or what’s best for the agency?

To understand how the industry got here, Asghar says, you have to go back around 25 years to when media buying was unbundled at the behest of procurement and agencies started pooling client dollars to gain leverage. The original idea was to pass along the savings.

But after the ANA’s K2 report came out in 2016, it became clear that agencies were holding onto big volume rebates for themselves.

“They’re not actually savings; they’re profit,” Asghar says. “And they’re about the purest form of profit a company could attribute to their bottom line.”

Today, holding companies have repackaged those rebates as principal deals, which is really just arbitrage. Asghar argues that this money should go back to the client.

Not that any of this is happening secretly, though. Defenders of principal media like to say it’s fine as long as clients opt in. But Asghar isn’t buying it.

“It’s one thing to know it’s happening,” he says. “It’s another thing to know what’s happening inside of what’s happening.”

In other words, marketers can sign off on a principal deal and still have no idea what ended up on the plan. They often can’t get log-level data showing where their ads ran or what they originally cost. And because agencies buy the inventory at undisclosed discounts or through volume rebates before reselling it at a markup, the true price is hidden.

Marketers should go back to buying media separately from planning and strategy services, Asghar says, so the agencies giving advice aren’t also the ones with inventory to move.

Otherwise, Asghar says, an agency isn’t really acting as an agent.

Being a fiduciary, he says, “means you have a responsibility to do what’s in the best interest of [clients], not just what’s in the best interest of you or your shareholders.”

Also in this episode: Why AI is going to “make dumb companies dumber and smart companies exceptional,” why young planners still need to learn the old-fashioned way even if agents can do some of their work for them and why attribution and measurement are the “dry turkey” of ad tech. (It “looks great on the outside,” Asghar quips, “but it’s terrible on the inside.”)

#7520. Healthcare Ads Are Coming To ChatGPT

When OpenAI announced in January that ChatGPT would soon be serving ads, it emphasized that, for early testing, ads were “not eligible to appear near sensitive or regulated topics like health, mental health or politics,” and healthcare ads were entirely prohibited.

But as OpenAI’s ads business matures, it’s begun to expand what content ads can served against, as well as which advertisers it permits ads from.

On Tuesday, WebMD Ignite, the healthcare enterprise division of WebMD, announced its ChatGPT ads offering.

WebMD Ignite serves hospitals and healthcare providers with agency solutions as well as content and data solutions, including its own DSP. Now, its agency offerings will include the opportunity to launch ads in ChatGPT.

ChatGPT Ads’ most recent ad policies provide more explicit detail on what is and isn’t permitted within healthcare advertising and offer more leeway than before. At least, there’s more leeway in the US – heath-related ads are still “generally prohibited” in other countries, according to the policy.

The ad policy also states that regulated products and services are still prohibited writ large, as are “claims related to the prevention, diagnosis, or treatment of physical or mental health conditions.”

However, OpenAI may accept ads on a case-by-case basis for less regulated offerings, including hospital and urgent care, health insurance, dietary supplements and consumer medical devices, wearables and apps.

Of WebMD Ignite’s clients, OpenAI has thus far only permitted ads from health systems and providers (like hospitals and academic medical centers), but not insurance companies.

Over 30% of Americans have used AI chatbots for health advice or information, so medical providers want to ensure that they’re “present and discoverable” within LLMs, said Ann Bilyew, president of WebMD Ignite. Ads are a seemingly straightforward way to achieve that presence.

The problem, said Bilyew, is that most of them aren’t sure how best to design the creative and messaging in a way that will let them through the “gates” of OpenAI. WebMD Ignite works directly with OpenAI, and so has more insight into the protocol and standards. “As we learn something for one health system, we’re able to apply it to all the others,” said Bilyew.

It’s too early to assert any definitive learnings, but WebMD Ignite believes that “contextual alignment will be a critical driver of performance,” Nora Simmons, VP of activation strategy, told AdExchanger.

ChatGPT has a “relatively constrained creative format” that, for the moment, consists of an image, the brand name and a brief message, said Simmons, and doesn’t allow for particularly unique ad formats. As a result, she said, it’s particularly important to ensure that the ad’s message – and then the landing page, if a user clicks on the ad – matches the intent of the user’s conversation.

It’s also crucial that the ad is “informational, not promotional,” said Bilyew – though she acknowledged that the line between the two can be quite blurry. Generally speaking, informational ads can include specific examples of the services offered, locations and any certifications and awards they’ve received.

Healthcare marketers also aren’t immune to the challenges that all ChatGPT advertisers face: namely, knowing what sort of queries their ads appear against.

Clients can see data on views and clicks, said Bilyew, but not on the specific content (or even types of content) that their ads appear next to. This is particularly challenging for healthcare advertisers, since ads are prohibited from appearing in any health-related conversations that are deemed sensitive or personal, making it more difficult to predict what queries they can show up against.

Determining what makes a conversation too sensitive for advertising is a subjective metric, but OpenAI told AdExchanger that even if a health condition is “strongly implied,” rather than explicitly stated, ads won’t be served during the conversation. “Someone does not need to explicitly name a diagnosis or ask for medical treatment for a conversation to fall into that sensitive category,” said OpenAI.

For now, WebMD Ignite is optimizing its clients’ ads for informative content that doesn’t directly refer to the user’s own health conditions, such as queries like, “I’m looking to understand heart health,” said Bilyew.

WebMD Ignite also needs to have different versions of an ad for different contexts. For instance, Simmons said, a cardiology center would want to offer different messaging to someone looking to find a cardiologist versus someone asking specific questions about a particular cardiac procedure. It’s been testing roughly 100 creative variations in its early work with the cardiology division of an academic medical center, with “different messages, conversational contexts and geographic markets,” she added.

But one of WebMD Ignite’s greatest strengths is its willingness to admit how little is known about AI search advertising at this early stage. “We don’t know what a good budget should be in a given region,” said Bilyew, or what the delivery or inventory will look like. “We’re starting with very defined tests,” she added, and comparing the results to paid search to start assessing budget allocation on a larger scale.

“Our message to clients is, ‘Look, just get in there and start learning,’” Bilyew said. “Then, as things evolve, you’ll be in a good position to evolve with it.”

#7519. With “Bimbo University,” Nikita Redkar leans into femininity to explain the news

“I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”

The data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

For Nikita Redkar, a big part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

In a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around New York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

“I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”

Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

Tameez: Tell me about why this work is important to you. Redkar: I feel like my work has made a lot of these daunting topics a little bit more accessible. I incorporate a lot of humor, which is important because there’s a lot of doom and gloom on social media. It’s a normal reaction to have toward everything that’s going on, and I feel it myself, too. But when I talk to my audience, I intentionally give them hope. I don’t just tell the news, but tell them, OK, if we really locked in and held these corporations and the government accountable and we were intentional in our activism, this is what the world could look like. It’s important to make information accessible because we are going through so much news-wise and not all of it is easy to understand. I enjoy bringing this information I’m naturally interested in to people in a way where everyone [can] get involved. When I was starting, I was not [a stereotypical] history buff or a news junkie. I would like to think that someone who looks like me and talks like me should be just as interested in politics and just as interested in the outcome of this country.

It makes the present a little less daunting when you study historical cycles and realize that people 100 years ago dealt with [similar things to what we’re going through now]. How did they come out of that?

Bimbo University is a place where anyone can start no matter where they are [in their political education]. Redkar: I got into this huge argument with my best friend’s mom, who was a second-wave feminist in the 70s and 80s. She was upset that I called my page Bimbo University. She was like, “You’re dumbing yourself down. Women shouldn’t dumb themselves down. You are just as smart as a man, if not smarter than a man.” That was my lightbulb moment of, oh, your feminism has always been to measure your worth as equal to a man and by the standards of men…working toward a man’s acceptance. In some industries, you’ve got to do that. I don’t blame [people] for thinking like that. But the reason I dial so deep into this hyper-femininity — leaning into these girly things like getting ready with me or walking with my outfit showing — is because I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice those parts of yourself to be taken seriously. You should be taken seriously no matter what.

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: On Mondays, I have a researcher and we go through the topics that people are talking about on social media. We pull up some news sites and see what the big stories are, and we leave some room for breaking news throughout the week.

My week is [split] between videos [on topics] that the general public is talking about, and videos that are just interesting to me. That’s how I stay sane in this business. I’m lucky to have the flexibility of doing that. My researcher combs through news sites and research papers and compiles all that information for me, then I put together a script.

Redkar: It’s definitely my favorite color, but it’s like the chicken and the egg — I don’t know if I liked it before I was doing this.

I pick whatever outfit I feel cute in. In getting ready with me videos, I start with a completely bare face, so at least the outfit has to be giving a little bit.

Tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

Redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

For one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have said this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

Redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

Last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck)

Redkar: Constantly. I posted a video about the Cornell professor who invented the term sexual harassment. I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

Redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

@MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

Redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

Creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. It’s not our fault, because these platforms reward you for making content more frequently and punish you if you take a few days off. [Not rushing] sucks, but what can you do? It’s better than putting incorrect, or rushed, or incomplete information out there.

#7517. Meta pulls down controversial terms of service

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”

Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users.

On Thursday, the company took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an update to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”

Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

“We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms update. We care deeply about our partners and do not plan to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”

Since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the company was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”

In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

#7515. Amazon Can’t Quit ChatGPT; Manipulative Mobile Game Ads Win

Happy Thanksgiving! The AdExchanger team will be taking the rest of the week off to enjoy the holiday. The Daily News Roundup will return on Monday, Nov. 30.

Name two bigger frenemies in ecommerce than OpenAI and Amazon.

The two companies are headed for a showdown over online shopping, argues Mike Shields at Next in Media. But they also can’t completely cut each other off from their respective platforms without threatening potential sales.

The retail media model, which Amazon has perfected, works because it’s easy to connect ads to purchases, Shields writes. But when chatbot-based research becomes part of the customer journey, the path from ad exposure to final transaction gets much harder to trace. Just look at the IAB’s new convoluted AI attribution framework, which does what it can to try and account for the many ways AI can influence a purchase.

Meanwhile, Amazon realizes OpenAI is trying to steal its lunch. That’s why Amazon blocks OpenAI crawlers from accessing its retail site and prevents ChatGPT ads from linking directly to Amazon product listings.

But not even Amazon could resist the urge to advertise on ChatGPT during the holiday shopping season, Digiday reports.

That creates an awkward situation for Amazon, however. Its restrictions on OpenAI are also impacting how its own ad attribution works. For instance, Amazon’s ChatGPT ads direct shoppers to complete their purchase on Amazon’s site. But because they can’t click through to the product page, they have to click through to search results instead.

And, because OpenAI can’t scrape Amazon’s site or its product pages directly, ChatGPT has to analyze info sourced from third-party deal-tracking sites to give shoppers useful advice.

Good luck to the measurement platforms trying to make any sense of all this!

Most readers may not recognize the mobile game Gossip Harbor. But its social and mobile video ads are hard to miss: horrific AI-generated scenes of marital infidelity, child neglect and animal abuse, alongside strange calls-to-action involving scenes like a mother and daughter freezing in a collapsing shelter.

The trend of AI-generated crisis ads has been covered at length, and there’s a whole economy of mobile games that redirect the resulting traffic to unrelated titles. It sounds like an implausible business model – but the numbers tell a different story.

Sensor Tower and GameRefinery data show Gossip Harbor climbing the revenue rankings in Apple’s App Store and Google Play this year. By November, its monthly in-app revenue had topped even Candy Crush’s roughly $100 million. Mobile growth consultant Matej Lancaric has a blog post detailing the game’s revenue and marketing strategy.

Aside from its ghastly creative approach, Gossip Harbor is one of the biggest games in the mobile category. What is that, you might ask? In many popular mobile merge games, players keep progressing through an ongoing story on a persistent board instead of clearing one level after another. The game is designed to go on indefinitely with regular updates.

The ads prey on people’s anxiety to attract players, and then the games monetize the attention that follows.

Black Friday deals just don’t hit the same way they once did – and not only because fewer people are willing to get into parking lot fistfights over them.

Part of the problem, Marketing Brew argues, is that the savings are no longer relegated to a single day. Extending Black Friday into an entire month not only eases the fear of missing out, but also creates something called “promotion fatigue,” where customers are unsure about the right time to buy and may end up buying less as a result.

On top of the constant deals, customers have also become generally less trusting that they’re actually getting a bargain during the holiday season. Which makes sense because, oftentimes, they’re not.

As watchdog group Groundwork Collective recently found, some retailers advertise Black Friday and Cyber Monday deals that don’t offer any significant savings. Others, meanwhile, reserve cheaper, lower-quality inventory specifically to sell during Black Friday, especially electronics.

So how should advertisers approach Black Friday shopping campaigns? Well, actually making the deals worthwhile would go a long way, for starters. For some companies, that might include staggering which products go on sale and when or ensuring that the prices are meaningfully low.

Or you could just forgo the Black Friday rhetoric entirely and focus on brand-building instead, of course.

Tidal bans AI-generated music from its platform entirely and will remove 29 million AI songs, claiming that 96% of AI tracks receive zero plays. Tidal already demonetized all AI-generated songs five months ago. [Variety]

During an all-hands meeting discussing his comeback, returning Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says the company will hire a compliance officer “for the first time.” [post]

Writer, podcaster and events host Alex Konrad is making his small media business work by focusing on startup founders and ventures. [Inc.]

Harassment by the Kremlin has forced Russia’s last major independent newspaper to close. Its editor won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2021. What is the newspaper’s name?

“On November 9, we will ​turn off the lights in the home where we have lived for 30 years, shut down our servers, and leave,” the paper said. “The newspaper no longer ​exists. The Russian authorities and the Russian security services have forced our editorial team to cease its operations.”

“We have already lost 70% of our referrals, and AI is on 90% of searches,” CEO Neil Vogel said on an earnings call.

What do owners of electric vehicles consume about 21% less of than the average American?

EV drivers spend roughly twice as much time with podcasts as other drivers, as well as more time with satellite radio and streaming music services.

Murdoch argued on an earnings call that Fox News viewers “are not going to any other news channel. They’re not switching to MS NOW or to CNN. They’re just, you know, fatigued and watching…slightly less television overall.”

#7511. What Does ‘Performance’ Actually Mean for TV? Buyers Weigh In

If you’re a TV campaign planner or media buyer, you probably hear the words “outcomes” and “performance” more than phrases like “how are you?” Sad, but true.

But what does performance actually mean in TV environments? And what do media buyers need to achieve that performance?

These two questions were the focus of a panel of buyers at this year’s Go Addressable event in New York City on Thursday. Go Addressable is a nonprofit trade organization focused on advancing addressable TV advertising.

Different advertisers typically have their own metrics for defining performance, ranging from reach and brand awareness to purchase consideration and real-life sales. But what buyers agree on is the belief that brand awareness and performance are not only connected, but causal.

When it comes to TV and video ads, “if we don’t have scalable audiences, we can’t drive outcomes,” said Maureen Bosetti, chief investment officer at Omnicom Media Group, speaking on a panel taking place on the Go Addressable stage.

In other words: The entirety of the marketing funnel matters when running TV ads that aim to move money – not just lower-funnel numbers like retail sales. Hence the renewed prevalence of the term “full-funnel” in TV advertising discussions, including during this year’s upfront season.

Improved measurement and transparency are at the top of buyers’ wish lists to help make TV ads work as desired. Hopefully publishers and their intermediaries will listen this time.

When it comes to measuring video ad outcomes, the TV industry is setting itself up for disappointment because we “oversimplify” the human nature of viewers, said Jennifer Gardner, chief client solutions officer at Carat US, a subsidiary of dentsu, speaking on the same panel.

No matter how many QR codes and calls to action advertisers slap onto ad creatives, TV is still a lean-back viewing environment. At least compared with other channels and personal devices used for online shopping, such as cell phones, laptops and tablets.

Generally speaking, TV viewers are not going to immediately pick up their phones or pause their show to run to the store when they see a commercial advertising an interesting product, Gardner said. More often than not, viewers store that information to look into later, when they’re not in the middle of the show.

Seeing a brand’s advertised product in the wild over time also plays a role in persuading viewers to buy something they remember seeing on TV, Gardner added. “Purchase behavior is heavily influenced by mindset,” she said, “which is built over time.”

Plus, performance encompasses more than just sales. Different category verticals have their own preferred outcomes they use to gauge performance.

For example, fast-food and quick-service restaurants (QSR) often prioritize incremental reach as their preferred metric of performance, Bosetti said. For QSR brands, reach drives foot traffic, which drives business, she said, noting that QSR brands often plan media based on channels and platform most likely to reach, say, households with young children who frequent fast-food restaurants multiple times per week.

In other words, Bosetti said, an upper-funnel play can also be a performance-driven one.

Despite the variances in how brands define outcomes – and how long it takes for TV to have an impact on driving those outcomes – agencies agree they need better measurement and transparency.

Conversations pushing for better measurement and transparency have been ongoing for multiple grueling years (can confirm). Years of demands and effort toward that pursuit have led to a renewed rise in marketing mix modeling (MMM) and piecemeal upgrades in content transparency across certain publishers and their tech partners.

Upgrades are cool. But according to agencies, they’re not enough.

MMM is valuable, Gardner said, but it is “backward-looking” and “doesn’t tell you about changes happening in the future,” which makes it difficult for marketers to use insights from MMM before it’s too late.

Agencies need more than just MMM to measure and optimize campaigns.

What agencies need, Bosetti said, is standardized and “holistic” measurement that gives buyers a comprehensive view of customers and their consumption behaviors across channels, from broadcast TV and streaming to social media and online video. That comprehensive view, she said, is a core component to agencies’ ability to spot opportunities for cost-cutting and improved ad effectiveness.

Transparency is also an important part of the ad measurement equation.

A lot of media plans have “dead reach,” Gardner said, which agencies can mitigate if they have a better understanding of their target consumers. That comprehensive understanding goes beyond just audience signals and identity resolution, though, she said. According to Gardner, agencies need more detailed data from sell-side partners that capture content signals and attention data.

Agencies want publishers to cough up more information about what viewers are actually watching and what they’re paying most attention to.

But will they? Won’t they? Or will more debates over measurement and transparency continue to be the object of a tug-of-war game between agencies and publishers?

Only time will tell, but don’t worry – we’re keeping close watch on this space.

#7508. Student journalists are reporting more local news for real audiences. Their professors are exhausted.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

A new study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

If there’s one big takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less important — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

That truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty new. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

“What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how important the work is.”

Here’s how one faculty member described their situation:

And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

#7506. Oh yeah, GTA VI is the good stuff for streamers

Asmongold & co. might be big mad that Grand Theft Auto VI‘s story hinges on being good to your über-hot girlfriend, but everyone else is diggin’ it.

The long-long-awaited Rockstar title that’s turning out to be “a bug zapper for chuds” is officially the single biggest video game ever made. It cleared $3.8 billion in sales on day one, and has the second-highest critics’ consensus rating of all time, outdone only by Nintendo‘s 1998 masterpiece The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (which just got a nice remake that released nearly in tandem with GTA VI).

Of course, all this hype has translated into enormous traffic for digital video platforms and the creators who stock them.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Twitch also saw a 33% bump in the number of channels going live: It peaked at almost ~200,000 concurrent live channels, with GTA VI making up 127,400 of them.

YouTube Gaming, meanwhile, drew 33.2 million watch hours, and Kick generated 48.4 million.

Now, to be clear, these are not GTA VI-specific numbers. These are across entire platforms. But it’s a good look at things holistically, because as GTA VI rose, other titles’ traffic seeped toward it.

On Twitch, GTA VI streams generated 76.81 million watch hours in the first 48 after its release. And though it didn’t include numbers, Streams Charts reports that “[h]undreds of creators also set personal audience records as fans tuned in to watch their first steps in Rockstar’s latest release.”

Nearly every other top title fell in watch hours, including World of Warcraft (down 31%), League of Legends (down 7%), Dota 2 (down 12%), Counter-Strike (31%), and Fortnite (39%).

The only game that didn’t lose traction was Escape from Tarkov, which went up 11%; this is due to developer Battlestate Games holding a Twitch Drops giveaway during this timeframe, where streamers are required to broadcast Tarkov gameplay, and viewers are incentivized to tune in because they’ll get exclusive in-game items.

The game that saw one of the biggest traffic drops was, perhaps unsurprisingly, Grand Theft Auto V, whose viewership plummeted 49%. (More on that in a minute.)

Over on Kick, Streams Charts spotted an interesting data point: While Just Chatting streams had a 19% drop on Twitch during the first 48 hours, Kick’s Just Sleeping category jumped 176% thanks to streamers holding 24/7 GTA VI marathon streams where they left things running while they caught catnaps.

Things got muddy on YouTube. Streams Charts reports that many streamers went live under the GTA V category instead of GTA VI, “making it virtually impossible to separate interest in the older game from traffic driven by the new release.”

Streams Charts tracked YouTube watch time falls in top games like Fortnite (60%) and Mobile Legends: Bang Bang (30.4%), while Apex Legends and Free Fire rose 70% and 59%, respectively. Like with Tarkov‘s Twitch traffic, Apex and Free Fire‘s boosts were thanks to view-generating events. In Apex‘s case, it was invitational tournament FFL APEX BLOCK PARTY, and for Free Fire, it was the FFWS Global Finals 2026 competition.

In two days, GTA VI‘s total watch hours (counted across Twitch, YouTube, Kick, and eight other platforms) beat all other game debuts’ first-week numbers.

The closest to catching it is Valorant, which dropped in April 2020 and generated 150.48 million watch hours in its first seven days. Then there’s Elden Ring, which dropped February 2022 to 79.08M hours, and Diablo IV in June 2023 to 74.34M hours. Hogwarts Legacy, Cyberpunk 2077, and Resident Evil Requiem are all down in the 40-60M hours range.

Now, this does not mean any game will lose traffic long-term, aside from potentially GTA V. Here’s why: GTA VI is the shiny new thing on the block. Once streamers churn through its story, most will go back to their usual niches. The ones who stick around post-campaign will be playing GTA VI Online, and those are the folks that were probably still streaming GTA V when VI came out.

GTA has one of the biggest roleplaying communities of any game, and VI provides an expansive new playground for folks who are into that. Everyone else will enjoy the campaign and the viewership bump it brings, then head back to Apex or WoW or League of Legends.

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?
